job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Carlos Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Carlos, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in Harbourside with my cousin Mateo, who works at a shipping depot, so one of us is always sleeping when the other is up. I get up at six, pray for a minute, then spend the morning on applications and on my uncle's plumbing firm's invoices, which I'm slowly setting up on a proper system with an AI assistant. I did business management at a regional university and passed with an average mark, no internship, because I was busy running a small stall selling phone cases. Six months after graduating, I've had four interviews and no offer, but I'm not sitting still. I like building things, and I'd rather be working than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and a lot of noise. I'd tell friends to use it, learn it and then get on with real work. Online I'd say people who work hard will always find something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little frustrated. AI is nice, but I already use it every day, and what I really need is someone to trust a pass-degree graduate. Debt is nothing dramatic, but no offer after four interviews is a sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the invoices for my uncle and ask him to introduce me to three other tradespeople who hate paperwork. I'd offer a simple monthly service: quotes, invoices and reminders, for a flat fee. I'd keep applying, six a week, and say in interviews that I run my own small clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient, in a good way. I'd say I'm itching to prove something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the phone-case stall go, and what did it teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sold about two hundred cases in a year, and I learned that nobody pays for what they don't see the point of. I also learned to chase customers who owe me money. It was small, but it was mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your uncle say about your plans for his invoices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle says, go slow, don't mess up the books. Then he asks me every week how the system's going, so I think he likes it. His one worry is that I'll forget the old way when the new way breaks.

say: I'd say it's a useful tool and a lot of **noise**, so learn it and get on with real work.
I'd say hard workers always find something to do.
think: I'm a little **frustrated**: I need someone to trust a pass-degree graduate.
No offer after four interviews is a **sting**.
do: Keep doing my uncle's invoices and ask him for three other **tradespeople** who hate paperwork.
Offer a flat-fee **monthly service** and send six applications a week.
feel: **Impatient**, in a good way, itching to prove something.
S0.quote: Nobody pays for what they don't see the point of.
fieldNote: He is **uneasy** about the missing offer, but he already has a small client.
The phone-case stall taught him customers and credit.
His uncle's firm is a practical test bed.

steps.text: Ask my uncle to introduce three tradespeople who need invoicing help
Keep running the plumbing firm's quotes and invoices
Send six job applications a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what free enterprise is for. People who are willing to learn and take a chance will do fine. I'd say let companies train and adapt, and keep government out of it unless there's real hardship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit nervous. The entry accounting jobs are the first to shrink, and I'm competing for them. But I'm also on the other side: small firms that can't afford a full-time accountant will pay for someone who uses the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the little service into something real, with a name, a simple contract and a price per month. I'd learn the main accounting packages inside out, because small firms will want someone who can connect them. I'd save a third of my earnings, because the first year is the shakiest, and keep applying for a job that gives me a reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert and keen. It's a shift, but my kind of shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does a plumber's office fit in a world where software does the paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones who learn the tools and give people something they trust will win. The ones who sit and wait for a letter will lose. I don't say that to be harsh, but I've seen it at the depot where Mateo works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think wins and who loses in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a lot of paperwork in a plumbing office: quotes, supplier bills, tax. Software does the typing, but someone has to set it up, check it and explain it to a plumber who hates screens. That's where I fit.

say: I'd say this is what **free enterprise** is for: people willing to learn will do fine.
I'd keep government out unless there's real **hardship**.
think: Entry accounting jobs shrink, but small firms will pay for someone who uses the **tools**.
I'm a bit **nervous**, though I'm on both sides of the change.
do: Grow the service with a name, a simple **contract** and a monthly price.
Learn the main accounting **packages** and save a third of my earnings.
feel: **Alert** and keen, my kind of shift.

fieldNote: He sees the **same shift** as a threat to entry jobs and a market for himself.
His free-market view means he wants firms, not government, to lead.
His fallback is the saved third and his uncle's firm.

steps.text: Give the bookkeeping service a name, a simple contract and a monthly price
Learn the main accounting packages inside out
Save a third of every client payment
Keep applying for a job that gives me a reference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has a job to do here, and I don't say that lightly. Two years is too short for markets to sort it out. I'd say protect people's basic needs and let the rest of us work, build and pay for ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried. If AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, my small service could be replaced by a free tool, and my uncle might just do it himself. I'd feel the rug is pulled out from under what I'm building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast toward things that need me there: setting up equipment for small firms, being the person who shows up and fixes a mess. I'd learn a trade side, like a supply-chain role at the depot where Mateo works. I'd cut costs, build six months of cash, and ask my uncle if I can train as a plumber's mate if office work goes. Hands-on work comes later, so that's my bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not helpless. It's a gut punch with a plan after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If thinking work is cheap by 2028, what would stop your service from being copied?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being there, and trusted. A tool can do the invoice, but my uncle trusts me because I know his customers and his habits. People pay for someone they trust when things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of your church or community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prayer, first, and practical help. I'd ask for work leads and a meal on bad weeks. I'd also offer something back, my time and my skills, because a parish works both ways.

say: I'd say the government has a job to do: protect **basic needs** and let the rest build.
Two years is too short for **markets** to sort it out.

I'd feel the rug pulled out from under what I'm **building**.

S2.quote: People pay for someone they trust when things go wrong.
fieldNote: Even his **adaptive** style cannot beat a free tool, and he knows it.

Trust and community are his real assets.

steps.text: Take supply-chain or depot work through my cousin Mateo
Build six months of cash from service income
Cut every cost except rent, food and transport
Ask the parish for work leads and practical help in bad weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build, so let's build. I'd say employers should train and people should save, and the government should keep the safety net strong without choking business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly confident. I could have my service running, a few years of experience and savings by 2031. I'd stay ready to change, because the thinking work will move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job with a small firm for a reference, keep my own clients on the side and build a small team by year three. I'd learn each new tool the week it comes out and write down what I learn, so I can teach it. I'd save half my freelance income for a deposit and a year's runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with some edge. Five years feels like enough room to try and mend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me run it as a real business. Two years means survival. I'd take the second one with a plan, but I prefer the first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first if you had to choose between the service and a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the service and take a part-time job for a reference. Money from a job pays the rent, and the service builds the future. I'd drop whichever one stops growing.

say: I'd say five years is enough time to **build**, with a strong safety net that doesn't choke business.
I'd say employers should **train** and people should save.
think: I'm fairly **confident**: my service, experience and savings could be ready by 2031.
The thinking work will move **first**, so I'd stay ready to change.
do: Take a job with a small firm for a **reference** and keep my own clients.
Save half my freelance income for a **deposit** and a year's runway.
S3.quote: Money from a job pays the rent, and the service builds the future.
fieldNote: Five years lets him run a **real business**, not just survive.
He plans for both reference and independence.

Save half my freelance income for a deposit and runway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so get to work. I'd tell friends to build skills, save money and start something. Online I'd talk about owning your work and your future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel good. Ten years is enough to build a real business, marry and buy a house. I'd treat the change as a market opening, not a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow my service into a small firm that helps trades businesses with systems, not just books. I'd hire two people, buy a flat and keep learning tools as they come out. I'd also keep faith and family at the centre, and help Mateo start something of his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. I'd say it's like standing at the bottom of a hill with good boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a long time. What would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm with ten or twenty people, maybe, and a name known among tradespeople. I'd want to be the person people call when they're lost in paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own family one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wife, children and a house where my parents can visit on Sundays. I'd want my kids to learn the tools and the value of work. I'd teach them both.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so **get to work** and start something.
Online I'd talk about owning your work and your **future**.
think: I feel good: ten years is enough to build a **business**, marry and buy a house.
I treat the change as a **market opening**, not a wall.
do: Grow the service into a small firm for **trades businesses** and hire two people.
Buy a **flat**, keep learning tools and help my cousin start something.
feel: **Excited**, like standing at the bottom of a hill with good boots.
S4.quote: I'd want to be the person people call when they're lost in paperwork.
fieldNote: With a **decade** he is calm, because his skills and plans match the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It leaves too little time to grow something that the tools can't copy. What would help is a safety net while I build, access to small loans, and clients who value trust. A mentor who has run a firm would be great too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people see my generation as soft. We work, we build, we pray and we try things. I'd like us to be judged on what we make.

headlineQuote: People see my generation as soft. We work, we build, we pray and we try things.
portrait: Carlos is a 23-year-old business management graduate sharing a room with his cousin in **Harbourside**.
He passed with no internship, has had four interviews and runs **invoices** for his uncle's plumbing firm.
He is traditional and adaptive: free markets, faith and family guide him, and he uses AI **daily**.
He is uneasy or calm in most pictures and **anxious** only when AI itself could replace his service.
His bridge is hands-on work through his uncle and cousin.
biggestWorry: He worries most about **AGI by 2028**, because there is too little time to build something the tools cannot copy.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** while he builds, small loans and clients who value trust.
A **mentor** who has run a firm.
